title: Swachh Survekshan Awards 2025-26
subtitle:
President of India Smt. Droupadi Murmu Awards the Nation’s Cleanest Cities after the Swachh Survekshan 2025–26

AHMEDABAD (Mentor) – SANAND (Mentee), INDORE (Mentor) - DEPALPUR (Mentee) & TIRUPATI (Mentor) - KUPPAM (Mentee) rank top 3 in ‘Swachh Shehar Jodi category for accelerating urban waste management excellence

NAVI MUMBAI, SURAT & VIJAYAWADA Declared Top 3 in Clean Cities of Super Swachh League
GVMC VISAKHAPATNAM, JABALPUR and LUCKNOW Emerge as India’s top 3 Swachh Shehar in the Million Plus population category

This year awards were given for the first time to Swachh River Front Town, Swachh Coastal Town and Clean Himalayan City,

350+ ULBs jump 500 ranks to move up in Swachh Survekshan 2025-26

Smaller Cities Lead the Change: 1,700+ ULBs with population under 50k Improve Their Rankings Over 2024–25

State-Level Winners to Be Honoured in Award Ceremonies in respective States
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                11 NOV 2026 8:31PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Smt. Droupadi Murmu, Hon’ble President of India, honoured India’s cleanest cities at the Swachh Survekshan Awards 2025–26 held at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi, convened by the Department of Urban Development (DoUD), Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA). Winners were felicitated in the presence of Sh. Manohar Lal, Union Minister for MoHUA & Power and Shri Tokhan Sahu, Minister of State for MoHUA. This year
60
national awards have been announced, under 5 categories:
Swachh Shehar Jodi (SSJ)
Clean Cities of Super Swachh League
Swachh Shehar
in 5 population categories
Swachh River Front Town
Swachh Coastal Town
Clean Himalayan City
State First
Swachh City
Speaking at the event, Smt. Droupadi Murmu, Hon’ble President of India,
underscored that cleanliness cannot be achieved through the efforts of any single institution alone and requires active participation from all stakeholders. She emphasized the importance of citizen participation, behavioural change, administrative accountability, and sustained public engagement. Highlighting the need to inculcate cleanliness values from an early age, she called for integrating issues such as plastic waste management into school curricula and fostering continuous dialogue with children and youth. The President noted that meaningful progress in sanitation is possible when citizens, local administrations, and sanitation workers work together, and when the on-ground suggestions of sanitation workers and citizen feedback are given due importance. She also appreciated the Swachh Shehar Jodi initiative as a new dimension of collaborative learning, enabling cities to share innovations, test solutions, and support one another in achieving higher standards of urban cleanliness.
Addressing the gathering, Union Minister for Housing and Urban Affairs Shri Manohar Lal said
that under the visionary leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi, the Swachh Bharat Mission has evolved into a nationwide people's movement, transforming urban sanitation and encouraging greater citizen participation. Highlighting the progress achieved since 2014, he stated that urban waste processing has increased from 16% to 80%, while door-to-door waste collection coverage has risen from 44% to over 96%. He further noted that the remediation of legacy waste dumpsites has freed nearly 11,000 acres of urban land for productive use.
The Hon’ble Minister also encouraged States to conduct Swachh Survekshan competitions at the State level to rank cities and towns within their respective States, fostering healthy competition among Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) and encouraging smaller towns to improve their cleanliness standards.
Shri Manohar Lal highlighted the growing scale and impact of Swachh Survekshan, which has expanded from 73 cities in 2016 to 4,751 cities in 2025–26. He informed that 2.70 crore citizens provided feedback during this year's survey, while over 1,700 smaller cities improved their rankings and more than 350 cities registered improvements of over 500 positions. Emphasising the importance of behavioural change, the Minister said that the real success of Swachh Survekshan lies not merely in improving rankings but in making cleanliness a permanent habit and collective responsibility. He also highlighted the participation of nearly 2.10 crore citizens in Swachhata Hi Seva 2026, the benefits extended to around 17 lakh SafaiMitras through over 33,000 special camps, and the participation of nearly 4 lakh children in Gyan Yatras.
The Minister further highlighted several new initiatives aimed at strengthening collaboration and encouraging excellence in urban sanitation. He stated that under the Swachh Shehar Jodi initiative, 70 mentor cities have been paired with 191 mentee cities to facilitate knowledge-sharing and improve sanitation outcomes. He also referred to the introduction of special award categories for River Front Towns, Coastal Towns and Himalayan Cities, along with recognition across five population categories to ensure wider participation. Highlighting the PRAGATI-50 initiative, Shri Manohar Lal said that 50 cities would be developed as Model Clean Cities through technology-driven interventions and continuous monitoring. Congratulating all award-winning cities, urban local bodies and SafaiMitras, he reiterated the Government's commitment to making cleanliness an integral part of urban life and realising the vision of a Swachh and Viksit Bharat.
Sh. Satendra Singh, Secretary, DoUD, MoHUA, highlighted
how Swachh Survekshan has, over the past decade, strengthened the assessment and improvement of urban sanitation services while driving tangible on-ground outcomes under the Mission. Secretary, MoHUA, further mentioned that Swachh Survekshan is much more than an assessment; it is the collective voice of millions of people committed to the vision of a Swachh Bharat. He said, “today is a celebration of the outstanding efforts made by our cities and citizens in advancing the cause of cleanliness.”
The Swachh Survekshan 2025–26 results reflect a strong upward momentum across urban India, with over
350 ULBs improving their position by more than 500 ranks
. Smaller cities have emerged as key drivers of this transformation, as
1,700+ ULBs with populations below 50,000 population improved their rankings compared to 2024–25
, demonstrating that sustained efforts and citizen participation are accelerating the Swachhata movement across towns of all sizes.
Showing excellence in collaborative efforts and peer-learning,
Mentor city
Ahmedabad & Mentee city Sanand, Mentor Indore
&
Mentee Depalpur
and
Mentor Tirupati & Mentee Kuppam
, were declared the top-ranked jodis under
Swachh Shehar Jodi
award. The Top 3 Swachh Shehar Jodis have been identified based on the combined score of the Mentor City (SS 2024-25 awardee) and its paired Mentee City. It reflects the joint performance and collaborative efforts of both cities under the Swachh Shehar Jodi initiative, thereby recognizing mentorship outcomes along with overall cleanliness and service delivery improvements. The intention of Jodi award is that the best performing cities should handhold cities with low scores to improve their performance. The initiative started after 2024-25 award ceremony with the motive of
Each One - Teach One
and rooted in India’s timeless Guru–Shishya tradition, where knowledge, experience, and best practices are passed on from one city to another to collectively advance the journey towards urban excellence and cleanliness.
Maharashtra’s
Navi Mumbai
, Gujarat’s
Surat
and Andhra Pradesh’s
Vijayawada
emerged as top 3
Clean Cities of Super Swachh League
.
Marking the rise of a new generation of clean cities,
GVMC Visakhapatnam
,
Jabalpur
and
Lucknow
emerged as India’s top
Swachh Shehar
in the million plus population category.
Swachh Survekshan Awards 2025-26 expanded its coverage to include the Hills and Himalayan cities as well as River front and coastal towns.
Rudrapur
in Uttarakhand,
Jammu
&
Shopian
in J&K have been declared as the top 3
Clean
Himalayan Cities.
Riverfronts, coastlines and water bodies, are an integral part of the natural and cultural heritage. Their cleanliness is essential not only for environmental sustainability but also for the health and livelihoods of communities. In line with the same, the top 3 ranks for the
Swachh River Front Town
have been bestowed upon Rewa (MP), Bilaspur (Chhattisgarh) & Varanasi (UP) consecutively, while awards for
Swachh Coastal Town
went to Odisha’s Puri, Kerala’s Alappuzha
and Maharashtra’s Ratnagiri.
To recognize and reward excellence across States and Union Territories, the
State First Swachh City Award
was conferred on
30 top-performing cities
. Union Territories have been classified into two categories for awards: (i) Up to 5 ULBs and (ii) more than 5 ULBs.
As part of the 10th edition of Swachh Survekshan, Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) were assessed across 43 indicators covering 10 critical domains, including
Segregation, Collection & Transportation of Waste, Solid Waste Management, Visible Cleanliness, Access to Sanitation, Mechanisation of Desludging Services, Ecosystem Strengthening & Institutional Parameters, Used Water Management, Advocacy for Swachhata, Overall Welfare of Sanitation Workers, Citizen Feedback & Grievance Redressal
. Over 3,000 trained assessors undertook extensive on-ground evaluations nationwide, supported by real-time GPS-enabled monitoring. From evidence submission to verification, the entire assessment process was conducted through a fully digital, transparent, and rigorously quality-assured framework, ensuring credibility and consistency at every stage.

The webinar commenced with the inaugural address by Shri Krushna Chandra Panigrahy, Director General, BEE, who highlighted the significance of energy efficiency as a key enabler of sustainable development and emphasised the need for concerted efforts towards promoting energy-efficient practices across various sectors.

The sessions also provided an overview of India's Standards and Labelling Programme for appliances, highlighting its contribution towards promoting energy-efficient products and enabling informed consumer choices.
Further, the discussions focused on market trends and the impact of behavioural changes on electricity consumption, emphasising the importance of sustainable consumption practices and responsible energy use. The role of Demand Side Management (DSM) in transforming energy efficiency into a flexible grid resource was also deliberated upon, particularly in the context of optimising electricity consumption, enhancing grid flexibility and supporting the integration of renewable energy into the power system.
The webinar witnessed participation from representatives of the Ministry of Power, Central Public Sector Undertakings (CPSUs), manufacturers' associations, industry representatives, domain experts and other relevant stakeholders. Through these initiatives, BEE reaffirmed its commitment towards promoting energy-conscious behaviour, sustainable consumption and mainstreaming energy efficiency as an integral component of India's sustainable lifestyle initiatives, contributing towards a more energy-efficient and sustainable future.

The Government of India set up the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) on1st March, 2002 under the provisions of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001. The mission of the Bureau of Energy Efficiency is to assist in developing policies and strategies with a thrust on self-regulation and market principles.
A key objective is reducing the energy intensity of the Indian economy. BEE coordinates with designated consumers, designated agencies and other organizations. It recognises, identifies and utilises the existing resources and infrastructure, in performing the functions assigned to it under the Act. The Act also provides for regulatory and promotional functions.

title: India and Norway Explore Joint Technologies to Turn Industrial Waste into Resources for Sustainable Construction
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                11 NOV 2026 10:38AM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), India, together with SINTEF and Research Council of Norway organized the India–Norway Dialogue on
“Waste to Resource Solutions in the Cement and Construction Sector”
on 10 November 2026 at India Habitat Centre, New Delhi, bringing together representatives from CSIR Institutes, SINTEF, regulatory authorities and the cement and construction industries to explore collaborative approaches for sustainable waste management and resource recovery. The Dialogue was timely and inline with the vision set forth by the Hon’ble Prime Minister of India, Shri Narendra Modi and Hon’ble Prime Minister of Norway, Mr. Jonas Gahr Støre during the formers visit to Norway in May, where-in the India-Norway relationship was elevated to a Green Strategic Partnership, with circular economy, clean technology and research at its heart. The dialogue commenced with a welcome address by Prof. S. K. Singh, CSIR-CBRI, who welcomed the dignitaries and distinguished participants.
The inaugural session was addressed by Dr. Rama Swami Bansal, Head, ISTAD, CSIR Headquarters; Dr. Arvinn Gadgil, Royal Norwegian Embassy, New Delhi; Dr. Kåre Helge Karstensen, Chief Scientist, SINTEF, Norway; and Prof. R. Pradeep Kumar, Director, CSIR-CBRI, among other dignitaries. The discussions emphasised strengthening India–Norway cooperation through joint technology oriented proposals involving CSIR institutes, SINTEF and industry partners, with a focus on translating research outcomes into practical and scalable solutions.
Prof. R. Pradeep Kumar highlighted the transition from a linear to a circular economy and the need to transform construction and industrial waste into valuable resources. Potential applications of construction and demolition (C&D) waste, steel slag, fly ash, red mud and other industrial residues were discussed, along with challenges related to processing technologies, standardisation, economic viability and market acceptance.
The technical session on “Safe destruction of POPs and hazardous waste” was led by Dr. Kåre Helge Karstensen, Chief Scientist, SINTEF and Dr. Ramesh Kumar, Chief Scientist, CSIR-NEERI, which explored the potential of cement kiln co-processing for the environmentally sound treatment of suitable hazardous wastes, including Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), DDT and PCB-contaminated materials etc. While CSIR-NEERI presented India’s National Implementation Plan inline with India’s Stockholm Convention commitments, the 2025 CDW Rules and related regulations and legacy POPs inventory; the International experiences presented by SINTEF highlighted the potential of cement kilns to destroy hazardous organic contaminants under controlled high-temperature conditions while substituting conventional fossil fuels with waste-derived alternative fuels. The discussions also emphasised the need for appropriate technical protocols, controlled industrial trials, emission monitoring and regulatory compliance.
Research initiatives of CSIR-CRRI and CSIR-AMPRI showcased opportunities for utilising fly ash, copper slag, red mud, plastic waste, steel grit and other industrial by-products in road construction, geopolymer concrete, specialised aggregates and value-added construction products. CSIR-NEERI and industry representatives further discussed challenges and technological requirements for the safe management and disposal of hazardous waste.
A dedicated session on C&D waste recycling, led by Dr. Christian John Engelsen of SINTEF, highlighted international best practices, including recycled aggregate-based construction products, mobile recycling units and improved processing techniques for removing impurities. Prof. S. K. Singh, CSIR-CBRI, delivered a presentation on "Using Slags and Other By-products in Construction", highlighting their potential applications in construction materials and the importance of sustainable utilisation of industrial wastes.
The dialogue identified several priority areas for future collaboration, including the development of two to three joint India–Norway research proposals, pilot-scale demonstration projects for hazardous waste treatment, technical guidelines for DDT and PCB-contaminated waste disposal, advancement of waste-derived construction materials and strengthening industry–academia partnerships.
The programme concluded with a shared emphasis on strengthening bilateral research and technological cooperation, promoting circular construction practices and accelerating the transition towards sustainable, resource-efficient cement and construction sectors.

title: Sarbananda Sonowal Lays Foundation Stones for Projects Worth Rs 560 Crore at Visakhapatnam Port
subtitle:
Sonowal Dedicates Port Promenade in Visakhapatnam to the nation, open for public

New Contracts to employ about 500 local people

Sonowal ties projects to PM Modi's vision of Citizens as Active Partners of development

ministry: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways
date:

                11 NOV 2026 8:38PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Union Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW), Sarbananda Sonowal, in Visakhapatnam, dedicated a waterfront promenade at the Visakhapatnam Port to the public and laid foundation stones for four new projects, bringing the port’s package of new works to about Rs 560 crore.
The Rs 19 crore Port Promenade runs about 710 meters (2,330 feet) along the water from the Venkateswara Temple to the International Cruise Terminal and covers about 5.5 acres. The promenade gives residents a regulated, safe place to watch ships and port operations for the first time. "It opens up the port to the city,"
Sonowal
said. "This project is dedicated to the people of Visakhapatnam.”
The promenade has a waterfront walkway and two view decks, one a Titanic-style viewpoint, along with a park, a public plaza, a children's play area, a food court and visitor parking. It was built on existing port land without affecting cargo operations. Its location beside the cruise terminal is also meant to add to the terminal's appeal for cruise passengers.
Sonowal tied the project to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's vision of inclusive development, in which citizens are not just beneficiaries but active partners in building the nation. A port that was once closed to outsiders now invites residents in, he said, and the new terminal contracts will give about 500 local people jobs running its berths.
"Prime Minister Narendra Modi
’s
vision is a development in which every citizen has a place and a part to play,"
Sarbananda Sonowal
said. "A port that opens its gates to the people, and gives local youth the work of running its berths, is that vision in action.”
Sonowal also laid foundation stones for three contracts to operate and maintain existing cargo terminals, together worth about Rs 580 crores. They cover the WQ-1 and WQ-1RE berths; WQ-2 and WQ-3; and EQ-3. Operators must mechanise the berths with cranes and conveyors, with environmental controls, and will employ about 500 local people. "Through these projects, VPA will secure assured cargo throughput and achieve optimum capacity utilisation in these berths,"
Sarbananda Sonowal
said.
The Union Minister also laid the foundation stone for upgrading the port's sewage treatment plant from 10 million liters a day to 15 million liters, including a new 5 million-liter plant, at an estimated cost of about Rs 11 crores. Treated water is used for dust suppression, wetting roads and sprinkling at stockpile yards, and the upgrade supports the ministry's Harit Sagar green port initiative.
Sonowal said the port handled a record 91.17 million metric tons of cargo in the 2025-26 fiscal year, about 10% more than a year earlier and its fourth straight year of growth. From April 1 to Oct. 31, cargo rose by 4.44 million metric tons, or 8.88%, over the same period last year. "You must
beat last
year's target of 10% growth,"
Sonowal
encouraged the port employees as he spoke and interacted with them.
The initiatives were launched as Sonowal is going to speak at the 31st CII Partnership Summit–2026, which the Andhra Pradesh government is hosting on November 12 and 13, which is themed under ‘Navigating New World Order: Trade, Technology, Trust.’
The port has taken up four Public-Private Partnership (PPP_ projects worth about Rs 800 crores, which are under construction and expected to be commissioned by 2027. It has one of the deepest container terminals among India's major ports, with a permissible draft of 16 meters, and is shifting to a landlord-port model to cut vessel turnaround time and logistics costs.
Sonowal credited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's leadership for transforming Indian ports into world-class facilities as the country works toward becoming a developed nation by 2047. He described the day's projects, from a public promenade to a cleaner sewage system, as examples of the Prime Minister's call for development that includes every section of society.
"When citizens are partners and not spectators, development lasts," Sonowal said. "That is the spirit of Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Vishwas, Sabka Prayas, and it is the surest road to a Viksit Bharat by 2047.”
Sonowal also thanked Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu and the state government for their support.

title: From the Margins to Leadership
subtitle: Inspiring Journey Of Six Women From Telangana And Delhi Reflect Their Empowerment Through Safer Livelihoods, Entrepreneurship And Community Leadership Under NAMASTE
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                11 NOV 2026 6:30PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Women engaged in sanitation and waste management are increasingly emerging as entrepreneurs, decision-makers and community leaders, demonstrating how access to institutional support, mechanisation and livelihood opportunities can contribute to their socio-economic empowerment.
The inspiring journey of six women from Telangana and Delhi reflect this transformation, highlighting their determination to move beyond traditional occupational roles and build more secure, independent and dignified futures for themselves and their communities.
In Siricilla, Telangana, five women sanitation workers
Anusha Reddy, Kavitha Goud, Swathi Yadav, Srilatha Naidu and Madhavi Kumar (all names changed)
had been working as septic tank cleaning helpers under private contractors. Each earned an average monthly income of approximately ₹15,000 while undertaking physically demanding sanitation-related work involving occupational risks and limited opportunities for professional advancement. Despite their experience in sanitation services, financial constraints and limited access to resources made it difficult for them to establish an independent enterprise.
A significant turning point came when the five women learned about the Swachhta Udyami Yojana (SUY) during a locally organised loan mela. Recognising the opportunity to become entrepreneurs, they collectively decided to establish a mechanised sanitation enterprise. With financial assistance under the scheme, they acquired mechanised desludging vehicles and began providing sanitation services under Siricilla Municipal Corporation. This marked an important transition from working as sanitation helpers to collectively owning and managing mechanised sanitation operations.
Through mechanisation, the women moved towards safer and more efficient sanitation practices, reducing their dependence on hazardous manual cleaning methods. Their responsibilities expanded to operating mechanised vehicles, coordinating desludging services and managing their enterprise. The initiative strengthened their economic independence, enhanced their professional confidence and enabled them to take greater ownership of their livelihoods.
Today, Anusha, Kavitha, Swathi, Srilatha and Madhavi are contributing to improved sanitation services while demonstrating the potential of women-led enterprises in the sector.
A similar journey of empowerment and leadership can be seen in Seemapuri, Delhi, through the experiences of
Anita (name changed),
originally from Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh. After moving to Delhi following her marriage, she began supporting her family by sorting waste alongside her husband, who was engaged in waste picking. Over time, she gained experience in waste management activities and started operating a small scrap shop, contributing to her family's financial stability.
Her journey towards community leadership began when she was mobilised by a Resource Organisation and became associated with a Self Help Group (SHG). Through active participation and commitment to collective development, she gradually emerged as a community leader and became the President of the SHG. Recognising her leadership abilities and experience, a local NGO subsequently engaged her as a Senior SHG Mobiliser and Community Mobiliser, providing her with an opportunity to support other women and waste pickers in accessing information, resources and institutional assistance.
Anita's association with the National Action for Mechanised Sanitation Ecosystem (NAMASTE) Scheme further strengthened her journey towards safer working conditions and socio-economic security. Through the scheme, she received occupational safety training, Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) and an Ayushman card, supporting her access to safer occupational practices and healthcare benefits. Her engagement with the NGO also enabled her to earn an additional monthly income of ₹10,000 while continuing her involvement in waste picking activities, contributing to greater financial stability for her family.
Drawing upon her own experiences, Anita now plays an active role in mobilising waste pickers, strengthening community groups and spreading awareness about the NAMASTE Scheme. She sensitises fellow workers about registration procedures, occupational safety measures and available government benefits, helping them connect with formal support systems. Her transition from waste picker to SHG President and community mobiliser reflects how access to opportunities, collective participation and institutional recognition can strengthen women's leadership and enable them to support the development of their communities.
The journey of these six women demonstrate the wider impact of interventions aimed at strengthening the safety, dignity and socio-economic empowerment of sanitation workers and waste pickers. While the five women from Telangana have moved towards collective entrepreneurship through mechanised sanitation services, Anita has emerged as a community leader, supporting fellow workers in accessing information, entitlements and livelihood opportunities.

content:
Bharat Parv 2026, organised by the Ministry of Tourism, Government of India, in partnership with Gujarat Tourism and with the support of States and Union Territories, is underway at Ekta Nagar, Gujarat, celebrating India’s rich cultural heritage, vibrant traditions and diversity under the unifying theme of ‘Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat’. The festival was inaugurated by Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi on 30 October 2026, as part of the celebrations of Rashtriya Ekta Diwas, and will continue till 15 November 2026.
The festival brings together traditional arts, handicrafts, regional cuisines, folk traditions, music, dance and indigenous craftsmanship from across the country, offering visitors an opportunity to experience India’s cultural diversity at one destination.
A major attraction of Bharat Parv is the Theme Pavilion, featuring participation from 29 States and Union Territories, Incredible India and Central Cottage Industries. The pavilion showcases more than 100 One District One Product (ODOP) products, along with traditional handicrafts, textiles, paintings, agricultural produce and other distinctive regional products, highlighting the artistic excellence and cultural identity of different regions of India.
The ODOP showcases are a key highlight of the festival, with participating States and Union Territories presenting products that reflect the distinctive skills, traditional craftsmanship and local specialities of their respective regions. From intricately crafted textiles and handloom products to traditional paintings, handicrafts and region-specific agricultural produce, these exhibits offer visitors a glimpse of India’s diverse indigenous products and craft traditions. By bringing locally renowned products onto a national platform, Bharat Parv provides an opportunity to enhance the visibility of regional craftsmanship, promote traditional skills and encourage greater appreciation of products made by local artisans and craftspeople. The Incredible India pavilion further highlights the country’s heritage, culture and festivals through engaging digital interventions.
Live demonstrations by traditional artisans are another major attraction, providing visitors an opportunity to witness India’s indigenous craftsmanship firsthand. These include traditional mask-making from Assam, Madhubani painting and Sikki craft from Bihar, Rogan art and traditional paintings from Gujarat, bamboo art from Chhattisgarh, coir-product making from Kerala, Pattachitra painting and silver filigree from Odisha, Aipan painting and Ringaal basket weaving from Uttarakhand, and Sozni art from Jammu and Kashmir. These demonstrations provide a platform for artisans to showcase their skills and introduce visitors to traditional art forms, techniques and indigenous knowledge systems passed down through generations.
The festival also features a vibrant line-up of cultural performances representing the diverse folk and classical traditions of States and Union Territories. Visitors are experiencing Kuchipudi from Andhra Pradesh, Bihu and other folk dances from Assam, Garba from Gujarat, traditional folk performances from Haryana, Tholpavakoothu from Kerala, Ravanhatta instrumental music from Rajasthan, traditional dance forms from Tamil Nadu, Santoor performances from Jammu and Kashmir, and Baul folk music and Purulia Chhau from West Bengal, among several other regional performances. These cultural presentations bring alive the music, dance and artistic traditions that form an integral part of India’s cultural heritage.
The Food Court, featuring regional cuisines and traditional delicacies from 23 States and Union Territories, is another major attraction, offering visitors an opportunity to experience India’s diverse culinary traditions. A specially curated Studio Kitchen, managed by the National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology (NCHMCT), further enriches the experience through demonstrations highlighting regional culinary practices and traditional food preparation techniques. The Food Court also hosts daily cultural performances from 5:00 PM to 8:00 PM, featuring artists from 10 States each day, combining regional cuisine, music and dance in a vibrant setting.
Beyond celebrating India’s cultural diversity, Bharat Parv provides a common platform for showcasing regional products, promoting indigenous art forms and bringing traditional artisans, craftspeople and performing artists closer to audiences from different parts of the country. The festival also highlights the role of local traditions, crafts and cuisine in enriching tourism experiences and showcasing the distinctive cultural identity of different regions.
Bharat Parv 2026 continues to reinforce the spirit of ‘Ek Bharat Shreshtha Bharat’ by fostering cultural exchange, promoting national integration and celebrating India’s unity in diversity. The festival will remain open to visitors at Ekta Nagar, Gujarat, until 15 November 2026.

The Ministry of Tribal Affairs will observe Janjatiya Gaurav Pakhwada across the country from 1 to 15 November 2026, culminating in Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas on 15 November, the birth anniversary of Dharti Aaba Bhagwan Birsa Munda. More than a commemoration, the Pakhwada is a focused, time-bound drive to accelerate the Ministry's flagship programmes, take their benefits to tribal families at the last mile, and build awareness of schemes and entitlements among tribal communities, students and citizens.
The Government of India designated 15 November as Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas in 2021 to commemorate the birth anniversary of Dharti Aaba Bhagwan Birsa Munda, under the leadership of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi. The day honours the contribution of tribal heroes to India’s freedom struggle and the lasting place of tribal communities in the nation’s cultural, spiritual and social life. Since then, Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas has grown into a national movement that celebrates the resilience and cultural diversity of India’s tribal people, and has given momentum to transformative programmes such as PM-JANMAN and Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan. During the previous 5 years, JJGD has been celebrated at Ranchi-2021, Khunti-2022 & 2023, Jamui-2024, and Dediapada-2025.
The 150th birth anniversary of Bhagwan Birsa Munda was observed as Janjatiya Gaurav Varsh in 2024–25, with over 28 national-level events and more than 2 lakh activities that drew over 3.8 crore participants. For tribal communities, Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas stands for recognition of their role in the freedom struggle and of their knowledge, art and harmony with nature.
During the JJGD celebrations for this year (2026), the Ministry has lined up a series of national events through the fortnight. List of the events planned as below:
On 12 November, approximately 200 students of Eklavya Model Residential Schools (EMRS) will interact with the Hon'ble President at Rashtrapati Bhavan.
The National Tribal Literary Festival will be held at India Habitat Centre, New Delhi, on 12 and 13 November with participation of Tribal writers from across the country,
National workshop at IIT Delhi “Strengthening Adi Vaani as Tribal Living Heritage and National Tribal Language Repository”.
The Rani Durgavati Adivasi Mahila Sammelan on 14 November will bring together 500 tribal women entrepreneurs from 30 States/UTs to strengthen market linkages and women-led enterprise.
The Swasthya–Poshan Sewa Sangam is holding health, nutrition and scheme camps for PVTGs at PM-JANMAN Multi-Purpose Centres from 15 October to 15 November.
Tribal Healers capacity building conclave with around 1,500 traditional healers from 9 States/UTs getting trained on 1 and 2 November in Hyderabad, under a programme to train and certify 1 lakh healers.
The Dharti Aaba Janbhagidari Abhiyan, through Adi Sewa Samay and Adi Sewa Din, will drive community participation in tribal villages, and about 1.54 lakh Adi Karmayogi Volunteers across 76,963 villages are being trained through State Administrative Training Institutes.
Scholarship Access Camps in 73 districts are assisting students with applications and Aadhaar seeding, and
A programme to conserve 200–300 medicinal plant species will be launched with CSIR-NBRI at Koraput, Odisha.
In addition to above, On Janjatiya Gaurav Diwas, over 300 projects for tribal communities across States will be taken up, with 228 ready for inauguration and 74 for foundation stone laying. These include a new Tribal Research Institute building in Itanagar, Arunachal Pradesh, and the Ropuiliani Tribal Freedom Fighter Museum at Kelsih, Mizoram.
Two national digital initiatives will also be launched. The Jan-HIT (Janjatiya Health Intelligence and Technology) Portal, developed with ICMR, is India's first platform for tribe-disaggregated health data, covering 20 States. The National FRA Digital Platform will bring the entire process of forest rights claims under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, from Gram Sabha submission to digitally signed titles, onto a single system.
Further, States and UTs are celebrating the Pakhwada through their Tribal Research Institutes, which have planned more than 160 activities in 19 States/UTs with an expected footfall of over 1 lakh people. These range from cultural festivals, exhibitions and tributes to competitions in schools, EMRS and hostels, and welfare and livelihood camps. Highlights include a statewide tribal carnival in Andhra Pradesh, the Adivasi Kala and Khel Samagam in Goa, a Bhagwan Birsa Munda Pavilion in Odisha, a Tribal Music Festival in Shillong and a tribal art and craft fair at Amdavad Haat, Gujarat. States will also hold Aadhaar and scholarship camps, sickle cell screening, Ayushman card camps for PVTGs, and legal literacy camps on forest rights.
The Ministry invites citizens to join the celebration by attending events in their area, taking part in the JJGD quiz and pledge on MyGov, supporting tribal artisans, and sharing their stories with #JanjatiyaGauravDivas and #JJGD2026.

title: Ministry of Tribal Affairs to Organise National Tribal Literary Festival in New Delhi on 12–13 November 2026
subtitle: Two-day festival to bring together tribal writers, poets, scholars and cultural practitioners; focus on preserving tribal languages, oral traditions and indigenous literary heritage
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                11 NOV 2026 7:44PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Ministry of Tribal Affairs will organise a two-day National Tribal Literary Festival on 12 – 13 November 2026 at Silver Oak, India Habitat Centre, New Delhi, as part of the celebrations commemorating Janjatiya Gaurav Divas 2026. The festival aims to provide a national platform for celebrating India's rich and diverse tribal literary traditions, promoting indigenous languages and oral narratives, and recognising the contributions of tribal writers, poets, storytellers and knowledge holders. The inaugural session will be attended by Shri Jual Oram, Hon'ble Union Minister of Tribal Affairs; Shri Durgadas Uikey, Hon'ble Minister of State for Tribal Affairs; Dr. Joram Aniya, Hon'ble Member, NITI Aayog; Shri Chamu Krishna Shastri, Chairman, Bharatiya Bhasha Samiti; and Smt. Ranjana Chopra, Secretary, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, along with other senior officials and distinguished guests.
The Festival aligns with the Hon’ble Prime Minister’s vision of Viksit Bharat@2047 by recognising the knowledge, languages and cultural contributions of tribal communities as vital to India’s inclusive, knowledge-driven and culturally rooted development, and by ensuring that their voices and heritage remain an integral part of the nation’s journey towards a developed India. It will bring together tribal writers, poets, authors, researchers, linguists, academicians and cultural practitioners from across the country to celebrate the diversity of tribal literary heritage.
Tribal literature represents an important repository of India's civilisational and cultural heritage. Rooted in community histories, lived experiences, relationships with nature, traditional ecological knowledge and collective memory, these literary traditions have been transmitted across generations through oral narratives, songs, folklore, storytelling and indigenous forms of expression. However, several tribal languages and their associated literary traditions continue to face challenges relating to documentation, intergenerational transmission and wider dissemination.
Recognising the importance of safeguarding this invaluable heritage, the Festival will explore the rich and diverse literary traditions of tribal communities, tracing the continuum from oral traditions and community memory to contemporary literary expression. The deliberations will cover the significance of tribal folklore, including, ritual songs, myths, folktales, riddles, proverbs, children’s traditions, seasonal narratives and women's oral traditions, as well as the role of oral epics and heroic traditions in preserving community histories and cultural memory.
The festival will feature thematic sessions on tribal literature, poetry, folklore and storytelling, bringing together writers, poets, scholars and practitioners representing diverse tribal languages. Discussions will examine the contribution of oral traditions to multilingual education, language and literacy, including their role in transmitting ecological knowledge, social and ethical values, and cultural identity across generations. Dedicated poetry and story-reading sessions will showcase literary works and creative expressions in different tribal languages, providing an opportunity for tribal authors and poets to share their narratives with a wider audience.
Through these literary sessions, the festival seeks to strengthen the recognition of tribal literary heritage, encourage the preservation and intergenerational transmission of indigenous narratives, and bring greater visibility to tribal languages and literary expressions in India's cultural and academic discourse.
Organised as part of the celebrations of Janjatiya Gaurav Divas, commemorating the birth anniversary of Bhagwan Birsa Munda, the National Tribal Literary Festival seeks to honour the rich cultural legacy and contributions of India's tribal communities. It reaffirms the importance of preserving and celebrating their literary and linguistic heritage as an integral part of India's cultural identity and collective heritage.

title: Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan at Six
subtitle: From Awareness to a People’s Movement
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                11 NOV 2026 12:27PM by PIB Delhi
content:
The
Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan
was launched on 15 August 2020 across 272 districts. It was extended nationwide to all districts on 15 August 2023. As of 10 November 2026, the campaign has reached over
35.84 crore people
. This footprint includes more than
14.33 crore youth
and
11.32 crore women
. Support services under the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR) have grown rapidly. Persons seeking treatment and counselling rose from
2.08 lakh
in 2020-21 to over
9.11 lakh
in 2025-26. As of 10 November 2026, more than
2 lakh
citizens have enrolled as Nasha Mukti Mitr.
A Movement of 35 Crore People
Under Article 47, the Constitution of India directs the State to endeavour to prohibit the consumption, except for medicinal purposes, of intoxicating drinks and drugs injurious to health. In 2018, a national survey showed that over 7 crore people in India suffered from substance use disorders, including nearly 1.2 crore children and 58 lakh women. Substance dependence harms individuals, families, and entire communities as a complex psycho-social-medical issue.
To address this challenge, the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment launched the
Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan
(NMBA) on 15 August 2020 in 272 districts identified as the most vulnerable to substance use (the use of alcohol, cannabis, opioids and other psychoactive substances). The districts were chosen from the inputs of the Narcotics Control Bureau and the findings of the first National Survey on the Extent and Pattern of Substance Use. It was expanded to 372 districts in August 2022 and extended to all districts of the country with effect from 15 August 2023. It is the flagship awareness programme of the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR), the Ministry’s scheme for prevention, treatment and rehabilitation. The Ministry describes this six-year change as a shift from organisational involvement to community involvement. States, districts and local stakeholders have taken ownership of the campaign, and that ownership has made it a Jan Andolan (a people’s movement).
NMBA has reached out to more than
35.84 crore people
, including over
14.33 crore youth
and
11.32 crore women
, as on 10 November 2026. More than 33.57 lakh awareness activities have been held in educational institutions. Its outreach has grown from 1.4 crore people in 2021. When the campaign marked five years at Amritsar on 18 November 2025, more than 6 crore people had joined its anniversary events at over 2.10 lakh locations, and it had reached 23.74 crore people.
The Scale of the Challenge
Article 47 of the Constitution directs the State to endeavour to bring about prohibition of the consumption, except for medicinal purposes, of intoxicating drinks and of drugs which are injurious to health. The Ministry has run a scheme for the prevention of alcoholism and substance abuse since 1985-86.
The scale of the task became clear with the first National Survey on the Extent and Pattern of Substance Use in India, conducted by the National Drug Dependence Treatment Centre (NDDTC) of AIIMS, New Delhi, in 2018 and released in February 2019. About
16 crore
people consumed alcohol, of whom more than 5.7 crore needed help for harmful or dependent use. About 3.1 crore used cannabis products and 2.26 crore used opioids, with about 25 lakh dependent on cannabis and about 77 lakh needing help for opioid use. More than 7 crore individuals were affected by substance use disorder, including nearly 1.2 crore children and 58 lakh women.
The National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme with central sector components. Its two objectives are to reduce drug demand through preventive education, awareness, identification, counselling, treatment and rehabilitation, and to reduce the stigma and discrimination that keep people who depend on drugs from returning to society.
How the Abhiyaan Runs
The Hon’ble Home Minister chaired the 9th Apex Level Meeting of NCORD in New Delhi to review the progress of NAPDDR and NMBA. While appreciating the efforts of all stakeholders of the Abhiyaan, it was directed to formulate a three-year action plan aimed at reducing drug demand in the country. To further institutionalise these efforts and ensure effective implementation, a three-tier monitoring and coordination mechanism was suggested. This mechanism comprises:
1.
State/UT-level Steering and Monitoring Committee
under the Chairpersonship of the Chief Secretary, which will meet quarterly and function as an apex body and a high-level task force with all relevant stakeholders and line departments for overseeing, coordinating, and monitoring all drug demand reduction initiatives in the State/UT.
2.
District-level Drug Demand Reduction Committee
under the chairpersonship of the District Collector/Deputy Commissioner, which will meet monthly and undertake mandatory quarterly inspections.
3.
Block-level Drug Demand Reduction Committee
under the chairpersonship of the Block Development Officer, to meet and conduct field inspections monthly.
Role of Three-Tier Committees
The roles of the three-tier committees are as follows:
1.
State/UT-level Steering and Monitoring Committee:
•    Provide overall oversight for implementation of the State Action Plan under NAPDDR & NMBA
•    Ensure achievement of quarterly and annual targets related to awareness generation, treatment, rehabilitation, counselling, capacity building and other relevant areas of action for drug demand reduction in the State/UT.
•    Coordinate efforts of Social Welfare, Health, Home, Youth Affairs, Women & Child Development, Higher Education, School Education, Skill Development, Panchayati Raj, Rural Development, Information & Broadcasting, Local NGOs/CSOs and other relevant departments.
•    Ensure integration of drug demand reduction activities into existing State/ UT programmes and schemes.
•    Review outreach activities conducted in educational institutions, villages, panchayats, wards, vulnerable communities, etc
•    Monitor implementation of Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (NMBA) and observance of key national events related to substance abuse prevention to reach more and more people.
•    Promote engagement of youth clubs, MY Bharat Volunteers, NGOs, spiritual organisations, and other relevant bodies/clubs/groups as Nasha Mukti Mitr (NMM).
•    Review availability and functioning of Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts (IRCAs), District De-addiction Centres (DDACs), Addiction Treatment Facilities (ATFs) and other treatment facilities. Monitor treatment admissions, recovery outcomes, relapse prevention measures and referral mechanisms.
•    Address gaps in accessibility and quality of treatment services.
•    Identify high-risk districts and approve focused intervention plans.
•    Direct special campaigns in emerging hotspot areas.
•  Review training programmes conducted for teachers, counsellors, healthcare professionals, law enforcement personnel, and community volunteers.
•    Review District performance against performance indicators.
•    Ensure timely reporting on the NMBA portal.
•    Direct corrective actions for districts showing persistent underperformance.
•    Facilitate optimal utilisation of Central and State resources for prevention, treatment and rehabilitation activities.
•    Encourage partnerships with NGOs, educational institutions and civil society organisations.
•    Any other matter with the permission of the Chair.
2.
District-level Drug Demand Reduction Committee
•    Prepare and implement a District Drug Demand Reduction Plan aligned with State targets.
•    Identify District-specific vulnerable populations and geographical hotspots.
•    Coordinate awareness programmes in schools, colleges, universities, workplaces and communities.
•    Ensure regular conduct of NMBA activities through departments and partner organisations.
•    Strengthen referral linkages between schools, communities, healthcare institutions and treatment centres.
•    Facilitate counselling and family support services.
•    Monitor the functioning of DDACs, IRCAs, ATFs and other treatment facilities.
•    Review admissions, treatment completion rates, follow-up services and rehabilitation outcomes.
•    Ensure availability of counselling, detoxification and rehabilitation services.
•    Conduct mandatory inspections of
✓    DDACs
✓    IRCAs
✓    Addiction Treatment Facilities
✓    Educational institutions undertaking prevention activities
•    Verify service quality, beneficiary records and infrastructure standards.
•    Promote awareness and preventive activities in villages, wards and urban settlements.
•    Encourage participation of Panchayati Raj Institutions, Urban Local Bodies, Self-Help Groups and faith-based organisations.
•    Validate District-level data relating to outreach, treatment and rehabilitation.
•    Ensure timely submission of reports through the NMBA portal.
•    Review onboarding, deployment and regular activities of volunteers. Ensure regular outreach in identified vulnerable communities
•    Facilitate convergence with Skill Development Missions and relevant departments for skilling and livelihood support of recovered persons.
•    Review and monitor the progress of skill development and rehabilitation initiatives for the recovered users in the district.
•    Any other matter with the permission of the Chair.
3.
Block-level Drug Demand Reduction Committee
•    Field-Level Monitoring of NMBA Activities
•    Monitor implementation of awareness and preventive activities across villages, wards, schools, colleges, and communities.
•    Ensure achievement of monthly targets assigned by the District Committee.
•    Map villages, urban localities, institutions, and populations vulnerable to substance abuse.
•    Maintain updated records of local risk factors and intervention needs.
•    Conduct monthly inspections of:
✓    De-addiction and treatment facilities like DDAC, ATF, IRCA, ODIC, etc
✓    Educational institutions conducting awareness activities
•    Verify the conduct and quality of activities reported.
•    Engage Panchayats, Urban Local Bodies, teachers, ASHA workers, Anganwadi workers, SHGs, youth groups and local leaders.
•    Promote community ownership of anti-drug initiatives.
•    Facilitate referral of individuals requiring treatment and rehabilitation services.
•    Support follow-up and reintegration efforts for recovering individuals.
•    Review onboarding, deployment and regular activities of volunteers. Ensure regular outreach in identified vulnerable communities.
•    Submit monthly implementation and inspection reports to the District Committee.
•    Escalate cases requiring District-level support.
•    Monitor compliance of institutions and stakeholders with directions issued by District and State Committees.
•    Ensure timely closure of issues identified during inspections.
•    Identify recovered persons requiring skill development
•    Facilitate enrolment and linkage of recovered persons with available skill development schemes.
•    Monitor beneficiary participation and provide regular progress updates to the District Level Committee.
•    Any other matter with the permission of the Chair.
States and Union Territories are encouraged to convene State, District and Block committees regularly, and the Ministry reviews implementation through monthly meetings, Chintan Shivirs (consultation meetings with State Governments, Union Territories and other stakeholders) and national conferences.
The Ministry provides
Rs. 10 lakh
to each district in a financial year as grant-in-aid for campaign activities, with later instalments released against utilisation certificates and progress reports. On the ground, Panchayati Raj Institutions, local leaders, Anganwadi workers, and ASHA workers carry out the work. Volunteers of the National Service Scheme and Mera Yuva Bharat (MY Bharat) take part alongside them.
The Union Budget provides
Rs. 333 crore
for NAPDDR in 2026-27. The revised estimate for 2025-26 is Rs. 420 crore, against Rs. 268.32 crore spent in 2024-25.
Strength from Spirituality: MoUs with Spiritual Organisations
Spiritual and faith-based organisations, with their influence among the members of the society, have been envisioned as one of the major stakeholders under the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan. MoSJE has signed MoUs with Brahma Kumaris, The Art of Living, Sant Nirankari Mission, All World Gayatri Pariwar, ISKCON, Shri Ram Chandra Mission, University of Patanjali, Sivananda Yoga Vedanta Dhanwantari Ashram, Adhyatm Vigyan Satsang Kendra, Chinmaya Mission, Divya Jyoti Jagrati Sansthan, Hare Krishna Movement, and Bosconet (Don Bosco) to leverage their networks for drug awareness. Through community events, school sessions, bike rallies, competitions, mobile vans, awareness runs, counselling, and meditation sessions, these organizations have reached over 7.72+ Crore people across the country. MoU with more organisations is underway.
The Sixth Year: Targets, Tools and Data
After August 2025, the Ministry set result-based targets for the campaign in six areas. They are training and capacity building of Nasha Mukti Mitr; evidence-based information, education and communication material; targeted intervention for vulnerable and at-risk groups; new faith-based and spiritual partners; coordination with line ministries; and quality de-addiction, treatment, rehabilitation and telemedicine services.
NMBA 2.0 App
The first NMBA mobile application was built to collect data on the Abhiyaan’s activities and show it on the NMBA Dashboard at the district, State and national levels. The NMBA website carried information on the Abhiyaan, the outreach dashboard, NMM registration and the e-Pledge.
The upgraded NMBA 2.0 App was launched on
24 April 2026
at the Chintan Shivir in Chandigarh. Citizens can take the e-Pledge on it, read awareness material, reach the helplines, and find the nearest de-addiction centre.
Monitoring Treatment
The NAPDDR Management Information System records every beneficiary at the supported facilities: registration, clinical assessment, substance use pattern, diagnosis, treatment and follow-up. The Project Monitoring Unit inspects centres through surprise visits, and the continuation of a project and the release of its grant depend on a satisfactory inspection report. Every organisation that receives a grant must be registered on NITI Aayog’s NGO Darpan portal and recommended by its State or Union Territory, and accreditation of grant-in-aid institutions is under way through the National Accreditation Board for Hospitals.
Data for Targeting
The First National Survey, titled “Magnitude of Substance Use in India”, findings of which were published in 2019, gave estimates of substance use at the national level and at the State level. The survey covered about 2 lakh households in 186 districts across all 36 States and Union Territories, and more than 4.73 lakh people aged 10 to 75 were interviewed. A second method, respondent-driven sampling, reached more than 70,000 people dependent on illicit drugs in 123 districts. The second National Survey, entrusted to NDDTC, will give district-level estimates for the first time, with results expected in 2027.
Schools and the Helpline
The life skills modules, developed by the Ministry for students of classes 6 to 11, equip teachers to teach life skills and drug education and to reach parents. The national toll-free helpline has been running since 1 March 2017, first as 1800-11-0031 and now as
14446
. It offers tele-counselling round the clock and refers callers to the nearest supported facility. It has received 5.10 lakh calls till date. It is integrated with two other national helplines. MANAS, the Narcotics Control Bureau’s round-the-clock toll-free helpline 1933, lets citizens report drug-related issues by call, SMS, chatbot, email or the web. Tele-MANAS, under the National Tele Mental Health Programme launched on 10 October 2022, widens access to mental health counselling and care.
Citizens as Nasha Mukti Mitr
Youth involvement has brought new perspectives, energy, and creativity to the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, playing a pivotal role in its success. As part of strengthening grassroots participation under the Abhiyaan, a Nasha Mukti Mitr (NMM) initiative has been launched to enable citizens to contribute actively towards drug demand reduction efforts. They are individuals who voluntarily register to support the Government’s efforts towards drug demand reduction and creating a drug-free society. Any citizen can enrol as a Nasha Mukti Mitr through the NMBA Portal and receive a certificate and the NMBA badge based on their level of participation. NMMs:
•    Spread awareness about the ill effects of substance abuse.
•    Encourage people, especially youth, to stay away from drugs and other addictive substances.
•    Help connect individuals or families affected by substance use with appropriate counselling, treatment and rehabilitation services.
•    Participate in and organise NMBA awareness activities, campaigns, pledges and community outreach.
•    Act as community-level change agents against substance abuse.
•    Promote the pledge, the NMBA logo, the mascot and the helpline 14446 in their communities.
The Ministry’s Abhiyaan page recorded more than
2 lakh
registered Mitr as on 10 November 2026. A Personal Dashboard launched on 17 June 2026 lets each Mitr track his or her own activities, access the IEC Material, and take the NMBA e-pledge.
The Nasha Mukt Bharat Saptah, observed from 17 to 26 June 2026 under the theme “Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan, Viksit Bharat Ki Pehchaan”, drew
1.31 crore
participants through pledge drives, rallies, competitions, street plays and yoga sessions. It closed at Haridwar with the extension of the MoU between the Department and the All World Gayatri Pariwar. The Ministry’s Abhiyaan page recorded more than 46.73 lakh pledges as on 10 November 2026.

Treatment and Recovery
Under NAPDDR, the Ministry supports a network of facilities of five kinds. There are
344 Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts
(IRCAs), 71 Outreach and Drop-In Centres (ODICs), 45 Community-based Peer-Led Intervention centres (CPLIs), 198 District De-Addiction Centres (DDACs) and 155 Addiction Treatment Facilities (ATFs) in Government hospitals.
•
IRCAs
provide inpatient treatment, counselling and rehabilitation.
ODICs
screen, assess and counsel, and refer people to treatment.
CPLIs
work through youth volunteers on early prevention among vulnerable adolescents.
•
DDACs
bring the services of an IRCA, an ODIC and a CPLI under one roof at the district headquarters.
•
ATFs
are set up in Government hospitals through NDDTC, AIIMS, which was entrusted with 150 of them, and through the Lokopriya Gopinath Bordoloi Regional Institute of Mental Health, Tezpur, for the North Eastern States.
The Ministry’s Abhiyaan page recorded
39.91 lakh
persons treated and rehabilitated as on 10 November 2026. The number of persons seeking treatment and counselling at supported facilities rose from 2.08 lakh in 2020-21 to more than 9.11 lakh in 2025-26, and more than 6.68 lakh recovered users have taken the NMBA e-pledge.
A Recovery at AIIMS Guwahati
Amit (name changed), a 31-year-old graduate from Kamrup Metropolitan district in Assam, reached the emergency department of AIIMS Guwahati after a heroin overdose. At AIIMS Guwahati, he was started on opioid substitution therapy, treated for Hepatitis C, and taken through relapse prevention therapy, with his family’s support, and the hospital’s Addiction Treatment Facility carried his care after discharge. He found work within two to three months of recovery and has stayed free of substance use for over a year. His medication is now being reduced under supervision.
Jammu and Kashmir: A Model with Potential for Replication
In Jammu and Kashmir, the campaign has reached more than
1.26 crore people
, including 72.26 lakh youth and 54.04 lakh women, and 11,152 Nasha Mukti Mitr have joined, as on 02 November, 2026. The Ministry supports an Integrated Rehabilitation Centre for Addicts, 3 ODICs, 2 CPLIs, 6 DDACs and 21 ATFs in the Union Territory, and the helpline has taken more than 11,000 calls from it.
Reviewing the Union Territory’s social welfare schemes on 22 October 2026, the Secretary, Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, described its coordinated, whole-of-government campaign against drug abuse as a model with potential for replication across the country. Under the Nasha Mukt J&K 100 Days Abhiyan, Addiction Treatment Facilities attended to more than 66,500 outpatients. Government Medical College, Srinagar presented a “Circle of Care” that follows a person from admission through treatment, rehabilitation, reintegration and long-term monitoring, and a proposed Rehabilitation and Socio-Economic Reintegration Scheme for Drug Abuse Victims, 2026, sets out a three-year recovery framework.
The Road Ahead
The second National Survey on the Extent and Pattern of Substance Use will give the country its first district-level estimates, with results expected in 2027. NAPDDR itself is being restructured after Chintan Shivirs and regional consultations with State Governments, non-governmental organisations, grant-in-aid institutions, experts and the line ministries and departments for health, education and prisons, and an expert committee is revising its guidelines.
Speaking at the third National Conference of the heads of the Anti-Narcotics Task Forces of the States and Union Territories in September 2026, the Union Home Minister said the country will collectively uproot the drug trade by 31 December 2029. He placed the protection of young people within the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047. The Abhiyaan is the demand side of that resolve: informed communities, early prevention, accessible treatment and reintegration with dignity.
Six years on, the Abhiyaan has grown from a campaign in 272 districts into a movement of 35 crore people, with more than 2 lakh enrolled NMMs and a treatment network of five kinds of facilities across the country. The helpline 14446 remains the first door for anyone who needs help.
